1985 → Today

Keep the
Internet Open.

A brief history of people building more freedom into our digital lives.

1985
Richard Stallman

Freedom to change the tools.

The GNU Manifesto asks for software people can study, change and share.

Open the original ↗
1985
David Chaum

A payment without a dossier.

Security and privacy can be designed together. Every transaction need not reveal your life.

Open the original ↗
1993
Eric Hughes

Choose what you reveal.

Privacy needs working tools. The cypherpunks set out to write them.

Open the original ↗
1993
Tim Berners-Lee · CERN

A web anyone can build on.

CERN releases Web software for general use at no cost. An open door for the next builder.

Open the original ↗
1996
John Perry Barlow

Imagine governing ourselves.

His declaration asks who gets to set the terms of life in cyberspace.

Open the original ↗
1999
Lawrence Lessig

The architecture sets the rules.

Software shapes what is possible. Its design can protect freedom or restrict it.

Open the original ↗
2007
Mozilla

Keep the internet open.

A public resource needs usable alternatives, open standards and institutions willing to defend it.

Open the original ↗
2008
Satoshi Nakamoto

Money without a central gatekeeper.

A concrete proposal for peer-to-peer payments, built from ideas others had begun.

Open the original ↗

What we do with that freedom

It has to work
in ordinary life.

I use the big platforms too. They save me time. I can live with some advertising. The harder question is how much of my work and my life depends on a service that can change the terms or close the door.

An open network gives us possibilities. Most people meet it through a product: a browser, a wallet, a place to keep their photographs. The easy option becomes the one we use. Leaving gets harder as our work, our habits and our people collect there.

I want to understand these technologies well enough to build useful alternatives. A parent saving a drawing should be able to choose where it lives and who can use it. They should be able to change the app without starting their family’s history over.

That is the work I want to take on: make that freedom practical enough to use.

Today
Solid · Tim Berners-Lee & collaborators

Keep the data. Choose the app.

A personal data store, with access you grant to the tools you want to use.

Open the original ↗

2026 / Where I’m starting

What a child makes
is worth keeping.

A drawing. A small discovery. A piece of who they were before they worried about who was watching.

I’m building ways for families to preserve those things and support the person making them. Tooth Fairy Network is my first attempt.

Keep the work → invite their people → attach a gift.

The direction: photograph a drawing, save it privately, approve a $1 gift to their vault. Make it easy enough to become an ordinary family moment.

The Solid connection is a local experiment: private artwork storage, selected-community read access and revocation have been tested on Community Solid Server. An early browser trial is available through the project page; hosted-provider compatibility is still being tested. No payments or promised investment growth.
